item.title: Trapped by a Partner’s Defensiveness? Change Your Response
item.description:
Relationships

Trapped by a Partner’s Defensiveness? Change Your Response

When you stop repeating the same patterns, the relationship has to change.

Posted August 21, 2026

In my last post, I shared an example of a woman who broke, mentally, physically, and spiritually. I described the moment when her body took over and announced that it couldn’t take it anymore, couldn’t take one more ounce of anger coming at her, that she had nothing left to give to make things work. It was the proverbial straw that broke the camel’s back, and the moment when the broken and dysfunctional system collapsed.

Sometimes we need to break to change, to be brought to our knees. But often we can make changes while we’re still standing, although we have to be willing to do things differently. If we don’t change our own behaviors, nothing will change.

The first step in getting free from this anger-defensiveness cycle is awareness. That is, to be able to see the patterns we’re acting out—how, in trying to stay safe and keep the peace, we’re actually playing a part in the continuation of this harmful pattern. Jumping to self-blame, still trying to figure it all out, making nice when none of it feels nice, smoothing the awkwardness, and making it all seem okay, like nothing happened—all of our fixing is just our part in keeping the broken system running.

After awareness comes acceptance. We must accept that our need to make things right and eliminate conflict may have become hardwired in us, and therefore not get caught up in judging it and ourselves, once again falling down the rabbit hole of self-criticism and avoiding the issue at hand: the anger and defensiveness. As a species, we need to survive, and deeply wired into us is the belief that maintaining relationships will make that possible. While this may not align with reality, our bodies still believe it, so we will do anything to maintain the connection with our partner, even if it means throwing ourselves under the bus for someone we may not even like or respect, and might even want to lose.

So too, we need to accept that what we’re doing isn’t working—that all the mental gymnastics, figuring out, fawning, and pretending it’s all okay doesn’t make any of this okay and doesn’t change the system, and won’t change the dynamic in the future. And we need to acknowledge that all our strategies are just Band-Aids for a systemic problem. Our efforts may put out the fires when they’re raging, but they don’t deactivate the cause of the fire.

Finally, we have to accept reality as it is, to recognize that anger and defensiveness hurt us. It’s not what we want in our lives. And yet, that is what we’re living, and often have been living for a long time. We have to get real with the truth: this is how we’re treated in our relationship, not all the time probably, but enough of the time for it to matter.

We have to be honest about what’s actually true and stop hiding from the reality. This is not someone else’s relationship—it’s our relationship, the person we’re choosing to spend our precious time with. This situation of anger and defensiveness is how we are choosing to live, as Mary Oliver put it, our one “wild and precious life.”

While we like to think of these episodes as one-offs and not that important, not the whole story, we still have to pull the lens back and look at how much of our energy goes into trying to get okay with something that’s not okay, making something work that’s broken, and taking responsibility for cleaning up someone else’s mess. And we have to accept that even if we think that none of this matters or counts in the grand scheme, our life is still passing by with this as our reality. This is where our energy and attention are being spent. This is our life—not the dress rehearsal. We don’t get this time back.

The last part of the change process is action. We have to change our own behaviors around anger and defensiveness—to stop fixing the situation when it’s not working, even though leaving it broken sets off every alarm bell inside us and goes against every intuition and protective cell in our body. Still, we have to shut our mouths, sit on our hands, stop smiling, leave the room, or do whatever we need to do to not make it all okay. To simply (but not easily) let the brokenness that our partner created just be, without taking it on as our responsibility to fix, to let the chaos be and not restore the peace. If we can do that for a few seconds or even a full minute at a time, that’s the practice, however small we start.

Simultaneously, we have to stop trying to mentally muscle our way through this, figure it all out, understand what we did wrong, and with more mental gymnastics, come up with yet another strategy that will change our partner and make them less angry and defensive. We have to remind ourselves again and again that this approach of figuring it out doesn’t work and hasn’t worked. We’ve tried it, and this problem is not something that we can figure out.

If our partner chooses to take responsibility for their actions, to change, then that will happen, but it’s not our failing for not being able to figure it out; it’s not something that our mind can figure out, and most importantly, it’s not something that we can change. At the end of the day, we have to stop taking responsibility for fixing what we didn’t cause. And maybe hardest of all, we have to be willing to live with the discomfort—and refrain from making it all okay. We have to sit with not okay.

When we take these three steps—awareness, acceptance, and action—something remarkable and profound becomes possible. As excruciating as it is to get there, we are, in a strange sense, rewarded for being brought to our knees, regardless of whether we were forced to adopt a new approach or have willingly “chosen” to shift. Firstly, when we stop rushing in to fix the situation and make everything okay, we have to actually feel what it’s like to be on the receiving end of this anger and defensiveness. We have to be with it as opposed to avoiding it by doing all the things we do to restore the peace.

The experience of feeling the pain of it, however, is our fire; it compels us to take other kinds of steps, and sometimes to say no and get clear about what we don’t want in our lives anymore. Even though it’s painful and unfamiliar, feeling the feelings as opposed to making the conflict disappear creates momentum for change.

At the same time, when we stop making everything nice and comforting, and stop reassuring them that they did nothing wrong and are not responsible for having hurt us, then we leave them to “hold the bag” for what they did and said. When we stop absolving them of responsibility, they’re left to claim it for themselves, and maybe even feel remorse. They may or may not feel anything like remorse, or change their behavior, but we’re no longer making it easy for them to deny what happened.

One thing is for sure: If we don’t stop making it okay for them to hurt us, they for sure won’t stop. Consequences can trigger change, so have the courage to let there be consequences, not just for you, but for them as well.

item.title: Are We Handling Young College Students with Kid Gloves?
item.description:
Education

Are We Handling Young College Students with Kid Gloves?

Are pass-fail systems helping or hindering first-year students?

Posted August 21, 2026

“My grade is an A-, but I almost have an A. Can you round up?” This question and similar grade-related questions have been asked of me several times throughout my nearly decade-long career as a psychology professor and director of a psychological assessment clinic.

In my first few years as a bright-eyed, self-conscious professor, I always held my breath when I submitted final grades. Students are paying thousands of dollars each year, racking up extraordinary student loan debt to obtain an education. I could at least do my part by giving them the grade they earned.

Recently, the University of Michigan’s College of Literature, Science, and the Arts announced the rollout of the Grade Covering Pilot Program for first-year students. For these students, first-semester grades will be recorded as a pass P or no credit NC on their transcripts. This is all done in an effort to “curb the mental health crisis” among young adult college students.

This pilot program misses the mark. Students need to know their standing in a course, and an official academic record, such as a transcript, should reflect that. Although the pilot program notes that students will still receive grades on assignments and instructor feedback, the simplified binary grading system eliminates the opportunity for academic distinction and merit recognition. Students may, in fact, contribute less effort knowing that they will earn either P or NC.

As imperfect as it may be, traditional letter grades are a helpful metric for student progress and tend to reflect the level of care, effort, and time students dedicate to the course. Moreover, it can reflect the instructor's ability to teach the information clearly.

While many first-year students are likely to be completing general education courses—which may be irrelevant to their major—some of these courses are foundational, making mastery of basic skills important. For example, when learning a foreign language, a student must develop certain grammatical rules and vocabulary words to advance to a higher level of learning. The same is true for first-year students learning computer coding, as they need to learn a new logic to understand one of the many core computer programming languages.

There is no doubt that the transition to college can be tough for young adult college students, and it has been eye-opening to observe how Gen Z is adapting to this adjustment. Gen Z college students are a particularly fascinating demographic because they are “digital natives,” experienced the disruption of their learning and education during their formative years due to the COVID-19 pandemic, and have consistently reported more mental health problems than previous generations.

These data indicate that Gen Z is struggling in ways we never expected. Although it has now been three years since the COVID-19 pandemic public emergency in the United States, it seems the consequences of this reverberate through the psyches of Gen Z.

Gen Z’s experience with loneliness, their yearning for social connection, and their preoccupation with their own mental health may be doing more harm than good. Their lightning-fast access to information allows them to mindlessly go down a rabbit hole where they spend hours and hours wondering whether their academic challenges are the result of ADHD, autism, or dyslexia, when in fact it could be lack of motivation.

As the director of a psychology assessment clinic, my job is to disentangle the complex concerns clients (many of whom are students) articulate and make sense of the challenges that they face on a day-to-day basis. In most instances, our clients’ concerns do indeed result in diagnoses, but there are several instances when clients do not meet diagnostic criteria for a mental disorder. In those cases, we sensitively explain to them that the stressors and concerns that they are facing are indeed valid, but that not every adverse situation or maladaptive response is attributed to a DSM-5 diagnosis.

Sociologist Tressie McMillan Cottom warns that the psychologicalization of everyday stressors or setbacks does more harm than good.

Moreover, it is difficult to keep pace with the perpetual “moment of rapid change in how people identify themselves and how many people feel empowered to identify and sort themselves,” explains Cottom. Colleges and universities are likely struggling to figure out the best way to address these issues; however, the pilot program just isn't the solution.

I am optimistic for the incoming freshmen at the University of Michigan. The University of Michigan is a highly competitive school with a 16 percent acceptance rate for undergraduates. Accepted applicants tend to have high averages—about a 3.8 GPA and SAT scores of 1389.

These are compelling statistics that depict a highly capable student body. During their four years of college, I hope these students embrace the enthusiasm and even lean into the uncertainty of their first year. I hope that they aren’t afraid to make mistakes as long as they learn from them. Sometimes the best ideas are born from mistakes and even catastrophes. I also hope that they give themselves and each other grace.

item.title: The Power of Uniting an Occupation Globally
item.description:
Career

The Power of Uniting an Occupation Globally

Lessons on connection and inclusion from an online, global 24-hour conference.

Posted August 21, 2026

Key points
  • Where there's a will, there's a way: you can build your global community from your own seat.
  • Specialization narrows our focus, but staying aware of the broader context enriches our perspective.
  • Stepping outside your silo helps you question your work and see the bigger system you're part of.

As organisational psychologists, we spend a lot of time thinking and talking about work-related issues across occupations and careers, but we rarely turn that lens on ourselves. One challenge of our own field is the name itself: depending on our country, professional body, or educational background (e.g., an undergraduate degree in psychology versus another field), we might call ourselves industrial, organizational (or organisational), business, occupational, or work psychologists—or some combination of these. Regardless of title, our goal is the same: making workplaces better for people, because we prioritise psychology and care about well-being.

G-WOP (Global Work and Organisational Psychology Conference) was initiated by a group of people who wanted to unite professionals whose occupational identity centers on this shared motive. The first conference was held in September 2025 and is returning this year with an equally strong programme. The amazing global meeting ran for 24 hours online (with sessions recorded and shared afterward, since nobody stayed awake the whole time). Supported by several professional bodies worldwide, it reached thousands of people, with talks on key and timely issues including AI in the workplace, leadership and identity, engagement and well-being, individual differences and assessment, and moral disengagement and ethics.

While G-WOP is a unique event focused on work and organizational psychology, its lessons apply to any occupation:

1. Global connection builds stronger occupational identities

The online conference was a chance to feel part of a global community and to connect with colleagues around the world. Any one of us inevitably focuses on a narrow set of tasks or responsibilities day to day, but as human beings, we usually find meaning in feeling part of something bigger. In a world this large but virtually connected, online events can help us find our global tribe. As one participant put it:

“The conference was a great opportunity to see the power of uniting work psychologists around the world, feeling proud of our identity together and showcasing the various areas where we contribute as scientists, practitioners, or both. It also showed that online conferences can work! I loved being part of it.”

2. Your area of work is richer than you think

To excel at our jobs, we naturally narrow our focus to specific interests, tasks, or responsibilities—a natural result of specialization and division of labour. But we shouldn’t lose sight of the broader context: we work, live, and function within a system where different actors and factors shape one another. Making the effort to step outside our silos and stay aware of that broader context enriches our perspective and pushes us to keep developing. To get inspired, enrich your perspective, question your ways of doing work, and start thinking outside the box, you need to know where to look and how to learn from others’ experiences. Online events might be great opportunities to do this with minimal cost and effort. As one participant put it:

“Being together on such an inclusive platform with people from all over the world with whom we share both theoretical and practical commonalities was not only emotionally but also intellectually fulfilling.”

3. Diversity and inclusion matter, and can be addressed in different ways

Many people lack the means or access to attend in-person professional events, whether due to financial constraints, visa restrictions, caregiving responsibilities, or health considerations. If we genuinely want diversity and inclusion, we can use technology to close that gap and G-WOP's own format is a good example of how. Running for a full 24 hours meant no time zone was structurally excluded, and recording every session let people join on their own schedule rather than requiring everyone to be online at the same moment. Small design choices like these can open a professional community to people who would otherwise be left out.

As one resource, William E. Donald’s book How to Organise Inclusive Conferences and Workshops offers clear guidance for academic settings that also carries lessons for non-academic environments.

4. We can bridge the scientist-practitioner gap in different ways

Bridging the scientist-practitioner gap remains a major challenge in our field: research has limited impact unless it’s grounded in real-world challenges and translates into results at work, while practitioners who adopt an evidence-based, scientific approach create more positive and sustainable impact. At G-WOP’s first meeting, 65 percent of participants placed themselves somewhere on a continuum between academic and practitioner, which stands as evidence of the conference’s power to unite scientists and practitioners in this field. That balance of research- and practice-based talks gave participants real-world examples and practical ways of combining science and practice. High-quality online events can also be good opportunities for improving mutual understanding and collaboration across people who prioritise different areas of work since focusing too heavily on one perspective can mean missing the potential gains the others offer.

Conclusion

I’ll close with a familiar idiom: where there’s a will, there’s a way. If you want to explore your global community, strengthen your occupational identity, connect with people elsewhere who share your background and motivations, and learn from their experience, you can do it from your seat—especially thanks to the efforts of people like Nikita Mikhailov, Michelle Goro, and Simon Toms, who believed in the power of bringing people with similar expertise, interests, and intentions together.

item.title: Three Options for When Your Child or Teen Breaks the Rules
item.description:
Parenting

Three Options for When Your Child or Teen Breaks the Rules

Exploring punishment, consequences, and collaborative consequence setting

Posted August 21, 2026

Key points
  • Punishment is sometimes necessary when children hurt others or engage in dangerous behaviors.
  • Consequences and reasoning can be used when children misbehave in more minor ways.
  • Collaborative consequence setting is useful with older children and teens.
  • It is important for parents to learn when to use each kind of intervention.

A colleague wrote to me about one of my most recent blog posts. In the post, I talked about the need for punishment and/or consequences when children or teens break a rule or behave in a way that the parents have told them not to. My colleague objected to my suggestion that punishment may be an option. He said, “I prefer consequences. Punishment for me evokes power.”

His email made me stop and think. Do I really approve of punishment? Is there a place for punishment in raising children? And if so, am I condoning parents using their position in the family to exert power over their children?

As I thought about this, I realized that I think there is a place for a whole range of consequences when children misbehave.

What happens when a child misbehaves

When a child or teen does something they have been asked not to do, the consequence for this can be relatively mild. For example, a child who fools around over and over again just before bed may be given the consequence of having one less book read to them that night. Parents will find that even such minor consequences can elicit a big reaction in small children. They may cry and carry on for quite a while when given such a consequence. But if a parent can hold firm and avoid the temptation to give in, they will soon find that the child takes their instructions to stop fooling around before bed more seriously.

With more important infractions—for example, if a child hurts another family member on purpose, whether physically or verbally, or if they do something which could be dangerous to themselves—this is the time that more serious punishment becomes an option.

Deciding when this is necessary is part of a parent’s responsibility.

It is a parent’s job to help their child grow up to be a considerate and well-regulated human being. It is the job of parents to keep their children safe and to convey the importance of abiding by certain rules of safety and human decency. In doing so, they sometimes have to impose certain rules and routines on their children.

Having this power is an awesome responsibility. And parents must always keep in mind that the use of their power must always be in the service of the well-being of their children.

​But when should a parent utilize punishment, when should a parent apply consequences, and when should a parent try to reason with their child?

This is the question every parent struggles with.

At a presentation given to the American Psychological Association, Robert Lazerle, Ph, D., said that research involving “...parenting interventions for young defiant children ha(s) found that timeouts and other types of assertive tactics can work if they’re administered correctly.”

He went on to say, “Punishments, such as timeouts or taking away something, were​ (shown to be) more effective than reasoning when dealing with a toddler who was acting defiant or hitting.”

He also said that the research shows that reasoning is not particularly effective with toddlers who are defiant or hitting.

And this makes sense. Toddlers have strong impulses and very little impulse control. When they are angry, they have very little ability to stop themselves from acting on their feelings. Some parents may like the idea of a gentler parenting style, and they may want to talk with their toddler about why we don’t hit or kick or bite...but it is often the case that the parent will find that this style is not so effective when it comes to impulsive acts of aggression.

​On the other hand, for milder behaviors, such as whining or constant negotiating, ​research shows that reasoning​, even with small children, ​can be helpful.

So it turns out there is a place for punishment, there is a place for gentler consequences, and there is also a place for reasoning.

Parents just need to understand when to use each form of intervention.

But, interestingly, there is also another option called “collaborative consequence setting.” Delany Rustin, a pediatrician, discussed this in a recent Screenagers blog post. She says that when an older child or teen misbehaves, the parent can try something new and ask the child what they think their consequence should be. She says that this increases the possibility that the child will actually think about why what they did was not OK. She also says that doing this supports children’s maturation, and it can result in kids being less oppositional and more kind as people.

With collaborative consequence setting, kids have less of an opportunity to think that their consequence is unfair, since they have a part in setting the consequence.

Proactive steps for parents

So here’s the take-away:

​1. With toddlers and small children, set strong limits around hurtful and dangerous behaviors.

2. Make it very clear to your child that hitting and hurting others is not OK.

​3. If your small child persists in hitting or hurting someone, tell them that you will help them to stop. Pick them up and remove them from the situation. If necessary, hold their hands so they cannot hit.

4. Once a child is at least three years old, you can start imposing brief time-outs if the child persists in hitting, hurting someone else, or doing something potentially dangerous to themselves. You can take them to their room, go in with them, shut the door, and tell them you will stay there with them until they calm down. You can talk during that time about how angry they were and how that made them feel like hitting (or kicking or biting or shoving), but how that is not OK.

5. If your young child is doing something that is just annoying, but not harmful, like whining or trying to negotiate with you, tell them clearly that you do not like whining or negotiating and it is time to stop.

6. As your child gets older, you can begin to involve your child in setting their own consequences when they misbehave. A child of eight or nine can participate in a discussion of what they think their consequence should be and why. And this can continue through the teen years.

So, in this post, I have suggested three options for responding to unwanted behavior in kids, along with the rationale behind each. Punishment can be used when a misbehavior is particularly hurtful or dangerous. Consequences and reasoning can be used for routine misbehavior, and with older kids and teens; collaborative consequence setting can be used when both parent and child have the time and motivation to sit together and discuss what happened and how to handle it.
